analysis.one_liner: Requires independent citizen commissions to draw congressional maps and bans mid-decade redistricting.
analysis.headline: The Redistricting Reform Act, backed by 61 House Democrats and no Republicans, has sat in the House Judiciary Committee with no hearing or vote since September 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take the drawing of congressional district lines away from state politicians and hand it to independent citizen commissions in every state. It bans mid-decade redistricting, meaning a state could not redraw its congressional map again before the next census unless a court orders it. It also sets uniform national rules: districts must follow the Voting Rights Act, respect communities of interest, and cannot be drawn to favor or hurt either political party. Members of Congress and state legislators currently control this process and would lose that control if it passed.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters — especially those whose votes are currently diluted by maps drawn to protect one party — gain a fairer and more transparent process. The bill requires public hearings, public posting of maps and data, a ban on considering where incumbents live, and rules that protect communities of color's ability to elect candidates of choice. Ordinary citizens can apply to serve on the commissions and sue to enforce the rules.

how_it_helps.text: Requires congressional redistricting in every state to be done by an independent commission rather than by legislators, with a three-judge federal court as a fallback if a state misses the deadline.
Prohibits mid-decade redistricting: once a state is redistricted after an apportionment, it cannot be redistricted again until after the next census unless a court requires it.

Bans maps drawn with the intent, or having the effect, of materially favoring or disfavoring a political party, using a defined test based on recent statewide elections and quantitative partisan-fairness measures.

Requires districts to comply with the Voting Rights Act and to preserve the practical ability of protected communities to elect representatives of choice, and to respect communities of interest and neighborhoods.

Imposes an open process: public hearings before and after draft maps, a public website with maps, data and software, disclosure of political spending by commission staff and vendors, and disqualification of lobbyists, officeholders and their family members from serving.
Bars map-drawers from considering where a sitting member of Congress lives, a rule directly aimed at protecting incumbents' seats.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the new commissions: the bill authorizes Election Assistance Commission payments of $150,000 per congressional seat, subject to appropriations. Political parties, incumbent lawmakers and state legislatures pay in a different currency — they lose their power to draw the very districts that determine who they run against, and maps favoring incumbents or parties would become legally challengeable.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes federal payments of $150,000 per Representative to run state commissions, a real taxpayer cost subject to annual appropriations, though states that draw maps with the politicians' own staff (like Iowa) are exempted from the commission mandate.
The process is elaborate and deadline-driven; if a commission or legislature misses it, a federal three-judge court takes over map-drawing, which moves a state's lines further from local control.

The partisan-fairness test — a rebuttable presumption of violation when a party's share of seats exceeds its share of votes by more than 7% or one seat in at least two of four recent elections — will generate heavy litigation and depends on courts accepting Congress's authority over a map-drawing power traditionally exercised by states.

Because the fairness standard measures party performance against statewide vote shares, states whose voters are geographically concentrated could see maps challenged even where they were drawn without partisan intent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — politicians no longer choosing their own voters — is large and goes straight at a practice that shapes every other outcome in Congress. The costs are real but secondary: some taxpayer funding, administrative complexity, and likely years of litigation over the fairness metrics. The strongest honest objection is constitutional: Congress is claiming power over a process states have traditionally run, and the bill itself flags that this would be tested in court. On balance the design is serious and detailed rather than symbolic, though nothing in it will ever be tested if it stays in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup and no vote since September 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 18, 2025 by Rep. Zoe Lofgren with a long initial list of cosponsors, all Democrats, many of them members of the California delegation.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary, and the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action.
It has 60 cosponsors in addition to the sponsor; every one is a Democrat and none is a Republican.

The bill's centerpiece, the ban on mid-decade redistricting, applies to redistricting already carried out after the 2020 census and would bar a state from redrawing maps again before the next apportionment unless a court orders it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The politicians and party organizations that currently draw congressional maps keep that power, because the bill never reached a vote. Members of both parties who benefit from maps already in place are better off with the bill stalled; the timing, arriving during a contested round of mid-decade remapping, means the present map-drawers retain the ability to redraw seats this decade.

for.name: Rep. Zoe Lofgren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited an initial cosponsor list of more than 50 House members, concentrated in the California delegation.

for.name: 60 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, bringing total support to 61 House members, all Democrats.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral in September 2025 and has taken no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: No House Republican cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the majority support needed to reach the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Support is 100% Democratic — 61 Democrats including the sponsor, zero Republicans — which mirrors the fact that the party holding the House majority benefits from the mid-decade remapping the bill would ban.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and national party organizations
industries.note: These officials currently control the drawing of their own district lines; the bill would strip that power, ban considering incumbents' home addresses, and make partisan-favoring maps presumptively illegal. Their interest in keeping the status quo runs directly against the public's interest in competitive, fairly drawn districts.

State lawmakers would lose the congressional map-drawing function their chambers now exercise, replaced by citizen commissions (with courts as a backstop), though states like Iowa that already use nonpartisan staff are carved out.

analysis.trajectory: With a referral-only record, no Republican support, and a Judiciary Committee that has taken no action, this bill will almost certainly die in committee at the end of the 119th Congress. Its realistic path to influence is as a template: the detailed commission structure and fairness metrics it lays out could reappear in a future Congress under different majorities, or in state-level ballot measures.
